newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark says 97 public surplus due to tightening.
newsitem.headline: Denmark says 97 public surplus due to tightening.

text.p: Denmark's Finance Ministry said on Tuesday the public sector budget would swing back into surplus in 1997 for the first time in nine years, attributing its forecast to fiscal adjustments, expected higher taxes and cyclical improvements.

In its latest budget forecast, the ministry foresaw a general government surplus of two billion crowns or 0.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) for 1997, improving further to a surplus of five billion crowns or 0.4 percent of GDP in 1998.
The ministry foresaw a 1996 public sector shortfall of 16.7 billion crowns.

The ministry's last estimates, announced in October, projected a general government or public sector budget deficit of 3.5 billion crowns or 0.3 percent of GDP for 1997, with a deficit for 1996 of 14.9 billion crowns forecast then.
"The improvement compared with the October estimate stems from fiscal adjustments made in the process of finalising the 1997 budget," the ministry said in a forecast booklet.
"Higher than expected tax rates at the local government level as well as further cyclical improvements have also contributed to the improved outlook for general government finances in 1997," it said.
It said a tight fiscal stance estimated at 0.5 percent of GDP had been instrumental in realising the government's objective of eliminating the public sector deficit.
"The 1997 surplus -- the first since 1988 -- is a first important step towards meeting the longer term requirements of a significant reduction in the relatively large government debt," it said.
The ministry put government debt at 603.9 billion crowns in 1996 or 59.7 percent of GDP, with the 1997 debt estimated at 611 billion crowns or 57.6 percent of GDP.

Overall state budget deficits of 25.0 billion crowns and 5.9 billion crowns for 1996 and 1997 respectively were foreseen in the latest ministry forecasts, compared to October's estimates of 28.5 billion crown and 19.3 billion crown shortfalls.

In late November, the Social Democrat-led minority coalition government signed a tactical agreement with the far-left Socialist Peoples' Party winning guarantees of its support for the budget, which will now be formally passed by parliament before the Christmas recess. --Chris Follett, Copenhagen newsroom +45-33969652
